source_text: I. Thesibus superioribus breviter & dilucide, quantum in nobis fuit, exposuimus doctrinam de Libero hominis arbitrio absolute & in se spectato, primo juxta Scholae Reformatae Doctores, deinde juxta mentem Doctorum Scholae Romanae. Ac ante omnia manifestum fecimus nullam esse controversiam de Libero hominis arbitrio circa quaestionem, An sit. Quandoquidem Reformati omnes fatentur non solum hominem, quum primum a Deo conditus est, praeditum fuisse libero arbitrio; sed etiam in homine lapso idem liberum arbitrium mansisse, nec in eo prorsus extinctum & amissum fuisse; quanquam per lapsum hominis valde infirmatum fuerit, & in servitutem peccati redactum, donec per Christi gratiam in libertatem asseratur.
english: The foregoing theses have set out, as briefly and clearly as we could, the doctrine of man's free choice taken absolutely and in itself: first as the teachers of the Reformed School hold it, then as the teachers of the Roman School understand it.

Above all, they showed that there is no dispute over whether man has free choice at all. Every Reformed theologian grants that man was given free choice when God first made him, and that the same free choice survived in man after the fall and was not wholly destroyed or lost. The fall badly weakened it and brought it into slavery to sin, until Christ's grace sets it free.

source_text: II. Secundo patet ex iis quae ante fuerunt a nobis exposita, utramque scholam in eo convenire quod liberum arbitrium non sit actus, aut habitus aliquis, sed ad facultates animae pertineat: neque tamen sit facultas quaedam reapse ab intellectu & voluntate distincta. Quae autem hodie de liberi arbitrii in homine natura quaestiones moventur alicujus momenti, ad hasce revocari possunt. Cujus facultatis respectu homo dicatur esse liberi Arbitrii? Deinde, Qua in re sita sit libertas a qua liberum in nobis dicitur arbitrium?
english: Second, what we set out earlier makes it clear that both schools agree that free choice is neither an act nor a habit but belongs among the soul's faculties, and yet is not a faculty really distinct from intellect and will.

The questions of any weight now raised about the nature of man's free choice come down to two. With respect to which faculty is man said to have free choice? And what does the freedom consist in, on account of which our choice is called free?

source_text: III. Quae vero circa quaestiones illas contentio superest, ut ex praecedentibus Thesibus liquere potest, non est proprie inter scholam & scholam; sed inter privatos Doctores qui, in utraque Schola, de hisce rebus varie sentiunt & Philosophantur. Quippe nulla prope sententia in una Schola circa haec obtinet, quae non habeat aliquos in altera Schola patronos. Et nulla saltem ab adversae Scholae Doctoribus rejicitur, quam domestici quoque aliqui non impugnent.
english: As the earlier theses show, whatever dispute remains on those questions is not really between one school and the other. It is between individual teachers who, in both schools, think and reason about these matters in different ways.

Hardly any view on them prevails in one school without having some defenders in the other. And at least no view is rejected by teachers of the opposing school without being attacked as well by some teachers of its own school.

source_text: IV. Etenim, ut hinc ordiamur, quum quaeritur ad quam facultatem spectet liberum arbitrium, magna pars Theologorum tum hujus, tum illius Scholae, censet libertatem humani arbitrii a ratione quidem originem quodammodo ducere, & suum habere fundamentum in indeterminatione, sive in αὐτοπραγίᾳ quadam judicii practici; sed tamen illam voluntati soli, tanquam suo subjecto inesse; quod Scholae dicunt libertatem esse in intellectu radicaliter tantum, seu tanquam in causa sine qua non, sed formaliter in sola voluntate. Adeo ut liberum arbitrium non aliud sit quam voluntas, sive simpliciter quatenus rationis judicium & dictamen sequitur, sive quatenus inter plura media a ratione commonstrata unum eligit, alterum repudiat; hoc admittit, vel non admittit.
english: To start here: when people ask which faculty free choice belongs to, a large share of the theologians of both schools hold that the freedom of human choice does in some way take its origin from reason and rests on the practical judgment's indetermination, or on a kind of self-action (αὐτοπραγία) in it, yet resides in the will alone as its subject.

The Schools put it this way: freedom is in the intellect only as its root, or as a cause without which it could not be, but it is formally in the will alone. On that view free choice is simply the will, whether insofar as it follows reason's judgment and dictate, or insofar as, among several means that reason points out, it takes one and refuses another, accepting this or not accepting it.

source_text: V. Verum sicut ab ista communiori sententia nonnulli Doctores Reformati recedunt, ita quoque & nuper, & olim, habuit illa in Schola Romana contradictores; olim quidem Durandum, nuper vero Gassendum, ex quorum sententia libertas non est in sola voluntate, sed etiam in intellectu; imo potius & prius in intellectu quam in voluntate. Quanquam fatendum est Doctores Reformatos in hac quaestione liberius versari, & majori cum diversitate sensuum & opinionum; dum alii libertatem ita communem faciunt voluntati & intellectui, ut tamen, juxta hos, ut Josuam Placeum, potiori jure ad voluntatem pertineat, juxta alios vero, ad intellectum, quae est sententia Mosis Amyraldi. Alii vero pertendunt libertatem non esse affectionem hujus aut illius facultatis, sed aliquid ex plurium facultatum concursu, & relatione mutua in homine oriens: adeoque subjectum libertatis proprie non esse hanc, aut illam facultatem, sed simpliciter hominem, quatenus intellectu & voluntate sua certo modo utitur. Ad quam sententiam nos quoque accedimus, quandoquidem homo liber est non simpliciter quatenus vult, nec simpliciter quatenus judicat; sed quatenus ex mentis judicio deliberato, & certo rationis consilio appetit & vult.
english: Just as some Reformed teachers depart from that more common view, it has also had critics in the Roman School, both long ago and recently: Durandus in the past and Gassendi now. In their view freedom is not in the will alone but in the intellect as well, and indeed more, and first, in the intellect than in the will.

Admittedly the Reformed teachers handle this question more freely, and their senses and opinions vary more widely. Some make freedom common to will and intellect, yet hold that it belongs with the stronger claim to the will, as Josué de la Place (Placaeus) does, while others give that claim to the intellect, which is the view of Moïse Amyraut.

Others insist that freedom is not a property of one faculty or another but something that arises in man from several faculties working together and bearing on one another. Its proper subject is then neither this faculty nor that but simply the man, insofar as he uses his intellect and will in a certain way. We take this view too, since a man is free not simply insofar as he wills, nor simply insofar as he judges, but insofar as he desires and wills on the basis of his mind's deliberate judgment and a settled counsel of reason.

source_text: VI. Quod spectat autem naturam libertatis, ut clarum etiam est ex iis quae praecedentibus disputationibus exposita fuerunt, non minor est in utraque Schola sententiarum varietas. Et primo quidem abunde probavimus, tam in hac, quam in illa Schola non deesse qui doceant, aliis reclamantibus, libertatem arbitrii oppositam non esse necessitati simpliciter, sed coactioni tantum. Verum illud quoque manifestum fecimus, quae hic est controversia, aut mere verbalem esse, aut saltem non magni momenti. Etenim qui affirmant libertatem in genere opponi non necessitati, sed coactioni solum, diversae sententiae Theologis concedunt, ad libertatem non sufficere immunitatem a coactione; nec libertatem in ea proprie consistere; sed in eo quod agens liberum seipsum movet & seipsum agit, ratione quadam agenti intellectuali propria, quae nec in rebus inanimis, neque in brutis reperitur.
english: On the nature of freedom, as the earlier disputations also make clear, opinion varies no less in both schools. First, we showed at length that in each school some teach, against the protests of others, that freedom of choice is opposed not to necessity as such but only to compulsion.

We also showed that the dispute here is either a mere matter of words or at least of little weight. Those who say that freedom in general is opposed only to compulsion, not to necessity, concede to theologians of the other view that being free from compulsion is not enough for freedom and is not, properly, what freedom consists in. It consists rather in the free agent's moving and acting itself, in a way peculiar to an intelligent agent and found neither in lifeless things nor in animals.

source_text: VII. Ac praeterea, quanquam existiment solam coactionem in agente rationali libertati officere, non vero necessitatem, nihilominus agnoscunt agentia libera in plerisque suis actibus, non solum immunia esse a coactione, sed neque esse ad unum necessitate quadam determinata. Adeoque inter actus creaturae liberae, ex eorum sensu nonnulli quidem necessarii sunt, sed plerique tamen contingentes.
english: Besides, although they think that in a rational agent only compulsion stands in the way of freedom, and necessity does not, they still recognize that in most of their acts free agents are not only free from compulsion but are also not fixed on one course by any necessity.
So, on their account, some of a free creature's acts are necessary, but most are contingent.

source_text: VIII. Unde est quod in agentibus liberis triplicem libertatem notant. Prima est quae dicitur in Scholis libertas contrarietatis, sive specificationis, per quam aliquis potest hoc, aut ejus contrarium, vel diversum agere. Secunda est quae dicitur libertas contradictionis, per quam, licet aliquis non possit hoc agere & ejus contrarium, potest tamen agere, & ab actione cessare. Quae utraque libertas opponitur necessitati, & determinationi ad unum, & comitem habet quandam actuum contingentiam. Denique his adjungunt tertiam libertatem, quae vocatur simplex sive complacentiae, per quam agentis liberi voluntas atque intellectus, dum in seipsa reflectuntur, vel tacite, vel expresse, proprios actus probant, & sibi ipsis quodammodo imperant; & ita ratione quadam peculiari seipsa movent, atque agunt; dum, scilicet, intellectus judicat se recte judicare, & sibi judicandum esse prout judicat; voluntas vero vult se velle, & in proprio actu seipsam figit atque firmat. Quae libertas esse potest sine libertate contrarietatis, vel contradictionis, & consistit cum necessaria, atque immutabili determinatione ad unum.
english: They therefore distinguish three kinds of freedom in free agents. The first, called in the Schools freedom of contrariety or of specification, is the power to do this, or its contrary, or something else.

The second, called freedom of contradiction, is the power, even where one cannot do this and its contrary, at least to act or to stop acting. Both of these are opposed to necessity and to being fixed on one course, and both go together with a certain contingency in one's acts.

To these they add a third, called simple freedom or freedom of complacency. Here a free agent's will and intellect turn back on themselves, tacitly or explicitly, approve their own acts, and in a way give orders to themselves, and so move and act themselves in a manner all their own: the intellect judges that it is judging rightly and that it ought to judge as it does, and the will wills its own willing and fixes and settles itself in its own act. This freedom can exist without freedom of contrariety or of contradiction, and it is compatible with a necessary and unchangeable determination to one course.

source_text: IX. Quum autem libertas extenditur ad actus necessarios atque immutabiles, fatentur illam latiori significatione sumi; libertatem vero strictius acceptam versari tantum circa contingentia, & quae possunt sic, vel secus se habere.
english: They admit that when freedom is stretched to cover acts that are necessary and unchangeable, the word is being used in a broader sense.
Taken more strictly, freedom deals only with what is contingent: with what may turn out one way or the other.

source_text: X. Qui vero contra pertendunt, libertatem opponi non coactioni solum, sed etiam necessitati, Theologis diversum sentientibus concedunt voluntatem, seu agens liberum, suorum quorundam actuum ratione habere se necessario; quamvis plerorumque aliorum respectu sese habeat contingenter. Ac praeterea quanquam existiment voluntatem liberam esse respectu tantum eorum actuum qui non necessario, sed contingenter ab ea eliciuntur, nihilominus agnoscunt in illis ipsis actibus ad quos voluntas immutabiliter & necessario determinata est, esse quandam voluntatis libentiam & complacentiam, quae in eo consistit, quod, dum voluntas in suum actum reflectitur, illum probat & sibi imperat, quatenus, scilicet, non vult simpliciter, sed etiam vult se velle, & in proprio actu acquiescit.
english: Those who hold the opposite, that freedom is opposed not only to compulsion but to necessity as well, concede to the theologians who disagree that the will, or free agent, stands necessarily toward some of its acts, though it stands contingently toward most of the others.

They also think the will is free only with respect to the acts it produces contingently rather than necessarily. Yet they recognize that even in the acts on which the will is fixed unchangeably and necessarily there is a certain willingness and complacency of the will. When the will turns back on its act it approves it and gives itself the order, since it does not simply will but also wills its own willing and rests content in its act.

source_text: [Print dittography, book 422-423: after X the compositor set 'XI. Unde patet, ut dixi, contentionem hic esse verbalem, non realem. Nempe utrique consentiunt quomodo res se in seipsa habeat. Nimirum voluntatem quorundam actuum respectu, habere se necessario; quamvis plerorumque aliorum respectu sese habeat contingenter. Ac praeterea quanquam existiment voluntatem liberam esse respectu tantum eorum actuum qui non necessario, sed contingenter ab ea eliciuntur, nihilominus agnoscunt in illis ipsis actibus ad quos voluntas immutabiliter & necessario determinata est, esse quandam voluntatis libentiam & complacentiam, quae in eo consistit quod dum voluntas in suum actum vel tacite, vel expresse reflectitur, illum probat & sibi imperat, quatenus, scilicet, non vult simpliciter, sed etiam vult se velle, & in proprio actu acquiescit.' and then set XI again in full, as follows.] XI. Unde patet, ut dixi, contentionem hic esse verbalem non realem. Nempe utrique consentiunt quomodo res se in seipsa habeat. Nimirum voluntatem quorundam actuum respectu, habere se necessario, aliorum vero respectu, contingenter. Illam respectu quorundam gaudere libertate contrarietatis, vel contradictionis: sed respectu aliorum esse ad unum determinatam, id est, non posse contrarium agere, vel ab agendo cessare. Et tamen in actibus illis quae necessario elicit voluntas, eam sibi complacere, & suos ipsius actus maxime velle & probare.
english: [The 1675 print sets this thesis twice. The first setting joins the opening words below to a repeat of the second half of X, adding only 'tacitly or explicitly'; the full thesis follows.]

This shows, as I said, that the dispute here is about words, not substance. Both sides agree on how the matter actually stands: the will stands necessarily toward some acts and contingently toward others. Toward some it enjoys freedom of contrariety or contradiction, while toward others it is fixed on one course, that is, it cannot do the opposite or stop acting.
And yet in the acts it produces necessarily, the will is pleased with itself and supremely wills and approves its own acts.

source_text: XII. Quaestio solum remanet, An actus illi quos voluntas elicit necessario, & inevitabiliter, & respectu quorum prorsus ad unum determinata est, liberi dicendi sint? Negant alii, statuentes eos nullo modo liberos, sed voluntarios solum dicendos esse, quoniam nulla ab ipsis nominatur libertas, quae non sit contrarietatis, vel contradictionis. Alii vero concedunt actus illos liberos quidem non esse, libertate strictius dicta, per quam possumus idem velle & nolle, sive diversum aut contrarium velle, aut saltem velle & non velle, sive a volendo cessare: sed nihilominus pertendunt eosdem actus liberos dici posse & debere libertate latius sumpta, quae est libertas simplex, sive complacentiae. Ita ut quaestio ad istud reducatur; An simplex complacentia, quae voluntati competit respectu omnium suorum actuum, sive necessarii, sive contingentes sint, mereatur, vel non, libertas appellari latiori quadam significatione? quae quaestio ut apparet solum est de nomine.
english: Only one question remains: should the acts the will produces necessarily and inevitably, toward which it is entirely fixed on one course, be called free? Some say no. They hold that such acts are in no way free and should be called only voluntary, because the only freedom they recognize is that of contrariety or of contradiction.

Others grant that these acts are not free in the stricter sense of freedom, the sense in which we can will and refuse the same thing, or will something different or contrary, or at least will or not will, that is, stop willing. But they insist that the same acts can and should be called free in a broader sense, namely simple freedom, or freedom of complacency.

The question therefore comes down to this: does the simple complacency that belongs to the will in all its acts, necessary and contingent alike, deserve to be called freedom in some broader sense or not? Plainly that is a question about a name only.

source_text: XIII. Et revera inter eos qui docent libertatem in genere oppositam esse non necessitati sed coactioni, id diserte affirmat Strangius Scholae Reformatae Doctor. Postquam enim multis docuit voluntatem liberam esse non tantum quum versatur circa media, sed etiam quum versatur circa finem, ac proinde Deum libere se amare, & homines libere velle esse foelices, quia libertas voluntatis in genere non est aliud quam spontaneum intellectuale: Et postea fassus est libertatem strictius etiam usurpari, prout versatur circa τὰ ἐφ' ἡμῖν, id est, ea quae sunt in nostra potestate, & restringitur ad media relata ad finem, aut ad ea quae parum, aut nihil ad finem conducunt, quo respectu libertas includit quandam indifferentiam, & actus liberi sunt mere contingentes; Deinde quoque observavit in hoc sensu a multis negari quod Deus libere se amet, & beati in coelo libere Deum diligant, concludit tandem his verbis, Neque nobis videtur hac de re litigandum, quia alioqui tantum esset λογομαχία, non enim negamus, sic vocem liberi arbitrii recte usurpari, quanquam in alio sensu illas actiones diximus esse liberas. De voluntate Dei lib. 3. cap. 14. pag. 687.
english: Among those who teach that freedom in general is opposed not to necessity but to compulsion, the Reformed teacher John Strang says this in so many words. He first argued at length that the will is free not only in dealing with means but also in dealing with the end, so that God loves himself freely and men freely will to be happy, since freedom of the will in general is nothing but intellectual spontaneity.

He then admitted that freedom is also used in a narrower sense, for what concerns τὰ ἐφ' ἡμῖν, the things in our power, and limited to means ordered to the end, or to things that contribute little or nothing to the end. In that respect freedom includes a certain indifference, and free acts are purely contingent. He further noted that many deny, in this sense, that God loves himself freely or that the blessed in heaven love God freely.

He finally concludes: 'We do not think this matter worth a quarrel, since it would otherwise be a mere war of words (λογομαχία). For we do not deny that the term free choice is properly used in that way, although in another sense we have called those actions free.' (De voluntate Dei, book 3, chapter 14, page 687.)

source_text: XIV. Inter eos vero qui docent libertatem oppositam esse non solum coactioni, sed etiam necessitati, idem agnoscit Guilielmus Estius Scholae Romanae Theologus. Etenim ad loca quaedam Bonaventurae contra sententiam ipsius objecta sic Respondet. Bonaventura quaest. 2. docet liberum arbitrium dupliciter posse considerari: vel ut liberum, vel ut deliberans: Et quidem quatenus liberum est, dicit esse posse respectu necessarii, sicut patet in Deo, & beatis; quia licet in illis habeat necessitatem immutabilitatis, non tamen coactionis. Quatenus autem deliberans, non est, inquit, nisi de contingenti, quia nemo deliberat de necessario & impossibili. Ex qua distinctione satis apparet, quo sensu dixerit liberum arbitrium quatenus liberum est, respicere etiam necessaria, & habere posse actum necessarium. Nam illud quatenus liberum, non aliud est quam quatenus voluntarium & non coactum. Itaque perinde est atque si dicatur, voluntatem quatenus libera est a coactione, versari circa actiones etiam necessarias. Illud vero, quatenus deliberans, id est, ut ipse exponit, quatenus consilians utrum eligat hoc, an illud; intelligitur de libertate quae propria est libero arbitrio ut tali. Igitur Bonaventura non in re discrepat ab aliis, sed minus commode, & praeter communem consuetudinem locutus est.
english: Among those who teach that freedom is opposed not only to compulsion but also to necessity, the Roman theologian William Estius grants the same point. Replying to passages of Bonaventure brought against his own view, he says:

'In question 2 Bonaventure teaches that free choice can be considered in two ways, as free or as deliberating. As free, he says, it can bear on what is necessary, as is plain in God and the blessed, for although in them it has a necessity of unchangeableness, it has none of compulsion. As deliberating, he says, it concerns only the contingent, since no one deliberates about what is necessary or impossible.

This distinction shows well enough in what sense he said that free choice, as free, also looks to necessary things and can have a necessary act. For "as free" means nothing other than "as voluntary and not compelled". It is as if he said that the will, insofar as it is free from compulsion, deals even with necessary actions.

"As deliberating", on the other hand, meaning, as he explains, as weighing whether to choose this or that, refers to the freedom that belongs to free choice as such. Bonaventure therefore does not disagree with the others in substance; he merely spoke less aptly and against common usage.'

source_text: XV. Neque majoris momenti videtur controversia quae in Schola Reformata manet inter illos ipsos Theologos qui fatentur arbitrii libertatem opponi non coactioni tantum, sed etiam necessitati: dum alii simpliciter docent omnem proprie dictam necessitatem libertati repugnare: alii vero concedunt quidem libertatem oppositam esse naturali necessitati, veruntamen pertendunt multiplicem necessitatem cum eadem arbitrii libertate consistere posse: nimirum agenti libero posse quandam agendi necessitatem imponi per efficaciam gratiae & providentiae divinae, aut etiam per mentis judicium practicum; quae tamen necessitas libertati nihil noceat.
english: The dispute that remains within the Reformed School, among the very theologians who admit that freedom of choice is opposed not only to compulsion but also to necessity, seems no weightier.

Some of them teach without qualification that every necessity in the proper sense conflicts with freedom. Others grant that freedom is opposed to natural necessity but insist that necessity of many kinds can coexist with that same freedom of choice. A free agent, they say, can have a certain necessity of acting laid on it by the efficacy of God's grace and providence, or even by the mind's practical judgment, and that necessity does freedom no harm.

source_text: XVI. Etenim qui pertendunt omnem proprie dictam necessitatem cum libertate pugnare, per necessitatem proprie dictam eam duntaxat intelligunt per quam agens, non tantum ad agendum determinatur, sed etiam quae tollit ab eo potestatem non agendi, aut aliter agendi, sive quae constituit agentem in eo statu, ut non solum agat certo & infallibiliter, sed etiam revera non possit non agere; idque non tantum in sensu composito, sed etiam in sensu diviso: ac proinde quae facit ut agens, sive dum agit, sive dum est proxime ad agendum paratus, non habeat talem non agendi, sive aliter agendi potestatem, qualis est in sedente, etiam dum sedet, potestas ambulandi, & vicissim in ambulante sedendi potestas, etiam dum ambulat.
english: Those who insist that every necessity properly so called conflicts with freedom mean by that phrase only a necessity that does more than determine the agent to act. It also removes his power not to act or to act otherwise; it puts him in a condition where he not only acts surely and infallibly but really cannot fail to act, and that not only in the composite sense but in the divided sense too.

Such a necessity would leave the agent, whether he is acting or is on the point of acting, without the kind of power not to act, or to act otherwise, that a seated man has to walk even while he sits, and a walking man has to sit even while he walks.

source_text: XVII. Itaque concedunt quidem motionem gratiae divinae, & providentiae quoque divinae efficaciam, aut etiam ultimum dictamen judicii practici, sic hominem ad agendum & volendum determinare, ut necessario sequatur actio quae libera dicitur, & impossibile sit ut posita providentiae & gratiae divinae motione & efficacia, non exeratur actus ille ad quem Deus sive per motionem gratiae, sive per providentiae communis efficaciam, hominem praeparat, movet, & determinat. Sed necessitatem istam non habent pro proprie dicta, quoniam cum illa stat vera non agendi potestas. Nempe Deus hominem, quem secundum propositum vocat, sic movet ad credendum Deo, & diligendum Deum & proximum, ut licet infallibiliter inde sequatur fides & dilectio, & posita tali motione, impossibile sit hominem non credere atque diligere, non tamen ab eo tollat potestatem non credendi, & non diligendi, quia cum motione divina non potest quidem compati actus illi contrarius, sed cum ea tamen consistit potestas ad actum contrarium. Non secus ac necesse est sedentem, dum sedet sedere, & ambulantem, dum ambulat, ambulare, & impossibile est ut sedens non sedeat, & ut ambulans non ambulet; & nihilominus manet in sedente vera potestas ambulandi, & in ambulante potestas sedendi; non quidem in sensu composito quasi simul possent ambulare & stare, sed in sensu diviso, quoniam quilibet actus, licet excludat actum oppositum, non tamen excludit potentiam ad illum.
english: So they do grant that the motion of God's grace, the efficacy of his providence too, or even the practical judgment's last dictate, determines a man to act and to will in such a way that the act called free follows necessarily. Once God's grace and providence are at work with their motion and efficacy, the act toward which God prepares, moves and determines the man, whether by the motion of grace or by the efficacy of common providence, cannot fail to be put forth.

But they do not count this as necessity in the proper sense, because a real power not to act coexists with it. When God calls a man according to his purpose, he moves him to believe God and to love God and his neighbour in such a way that faith and love follow infallibly, and with that motion in place the man cannot fail to believe and love. Yet God does not take away his power not to believe and not to love. The act contrary to the divine motion cannot coexist with it, but the power to that contrary act does.

In the same way a seated man must be sitting while he sits and a walking man must be walking while he walks; it is impossible for a seated man not to sit or for a walking man not to walk. Yet the seated man keeps a real power to walk and the walker a real power to sit. This holds not in the composite sense, as if they could walk and stand at once, but in the divided sense, because any act, while it excludes the opposite act, does not exclude the potency for it.

source_text: XVIII. Igitur, juxta hanc doctrinam, homo ad hoc vel illud agendum efficaciter a Deo motus, vel judicii proprii dictamine impulsus, necessario quidem agit necessitate quadam infallibilitatis; sed simul tamen veram non agendi potestatem retinet. Et potest quidem non agere, sed certo tamen acturus est: neque contingere potest ut carentia actionis conjungatur unquam cum tali judicio, vel cum ejusmodi Dei motione.
english: On this teaching, then, a man whom God effectively moves to do this or that, or whom the dictate of his own judgment drives to it, does act necessarily, with a necessity of infallibility, while still keeping a real power not to act.
He is able not to act, yet he will surely act; and the absence of the act can never be found together with such a judgment or with such a motion from God.

source_text: XIX. Qui vero contra docent multiplicem necessitatem cum libertate consistere, & illum quem gratia movet aut judicii proprii dictamen ad agendum impellit, non posse non agere, non aliud sibi volunt quam impossibile esse ut homo qui movetur a Deo ad aliquem actum, gratia illa quae in hominibus operari dicitur velle & perficere, vel saltem providentiae communis efficacia, aut etiam rationis propriae judicio, non eliciat actum illum ad quem sic supponitur motus & excitatus: adeoque ex positione talis gratiae atque auxilii & talis quoque judicii, necessario sequi hominem sic, vel sic acturum.
english: Those on the other side, who teach that necessity of many kinds is compatible with freedom, and that a man moved by grace or driven by his own judgment's dictate to act cannot fail to act, mean only this. When God moves a man to some act, whether by the grace said to work in men both to will and to do, or at least by the efficacy of common providence, or even by the judgment of his own reason, the man cannot fail to produce the act he is assumed to have been moved and stirred to.
So once such grace and help, and such a judgment, are given, it follows necessarily that the man will act in this way or that.

source_text: XX. Caeterum facile concedent, ab eo quem gratia movet, exempli causa, ad orandum, & eleemosynam pauperi largiendam, non omnino propterea tolli potentiam non orandi, & eleemosynam illam non largiendi; imo cum ipso actu invocandi & dandi eleemosynam non minus stare potentiam ad privationem illorum actuum, aut etiam ad actus contrarios, quam cum actu loquendi stat potestas silendi, & cum actu sedendi stat potestas non sedendi, aut etiam ambulandi.
english: Still, they will readily admit that when grace moves someone to pray, say, or to give alms to a poor man, his power not to pray and not to give those alms is not removed on that account.

Indeed, the power to leave those acts undone, or even to do the opposite, coexists with the very act of praying and of giving alms just as much as the power to keep silent coexists with the act of speaking, and the power not to sit, or even to walk, coexists with the act of sitting.

source_text: XXI. Utrique ergo in eo conveniunt, necesse esse ut agat ille quem ad agendum movet atque impellit divinae gratiae, vel providentiae vis & efficacia, & rationis propriae dictamen, quoniam ab illa motione Dei & judicii proprii determinatione actio hominis separari non potest: & tamen cum ejusmodi actu, adeoque cum motione Dei ad talem actum consistere potestatem ad cessationem ab illo, aut etiam ad actum oppositum, qua ratione saepius expositum & repetitum est.
english: Both sides, then, agree on two points. A man whom the force and efficacy of God's grace or providence, together with his own reason's dictate, moves and drives to act must act, because his action cannot be separated from that motion of God and that determination of his own judgment.
And yet with such an act, and so with God's motion toward it, there coexists a power to stop it or even to do the opposite, in the way that has been explained and repeated more than once.

source_text: XXII. Proinde quum isti quidem asserunt eum quem Deus movet ad actum hunc, aut illum necessario agere; alii vero pertendunt nulla proprie dicta necessitate illum ad agendum impelli, verbis quidem discrepant, idem autem reipsa sentiunt. Nempe priores dicunt ejusmodi hominem necessario agere, quia impossibile est actum ejus a divina motione sejungi, quod alii non negant. Juxta posteriores autem nulla proprie dicta necessitate ad agendum tenetur, quia cum ipso ejus actu, ac proinde multo magis cum motione ad actum, optime consistit potestas ad actum contrarium, vel saltem ad actus istius carentiam, quod priores facile concedent.
english: So when one party says that a man whom God moves to a given act acts necessarily, and the other insists that no necessity in the proper sense drives him to act, their words differ but their meaning is the same.

The first party says such a man acts necessarily because his act cannot be separated from God's motion, and the second does not deny it. The second says he is bound to act by no necessity in the proper sense, because a power to the opposite act, or at least to leaving the act undone, sits perfectly well with the act itself and still more with the motion toward it, and the first party readily grants that.

source_text: XXIII. Indidem quoque apparet facile componi posse dissidium quod adhuc superesse videtur inter Doctores Scholae Reformatae: dum alii, scilicet, affirmant libertatem arbitrii includere quandam agentis liberi indifferentiam, per quam positis omnibus ad agendum praerequisitis, potest agere, vel non agere, hoc aut illud agere; alii vero negant talem indifferentiam libertate includi, aut ad libertatem omnino pertinere.
english: The same considerations show that the disagreement still apparently left among teachers of the Reformed School can easily be settled.

Some of them hold that freedom of choice includes a certain indifference in the free agent, by which, given everything required beforehand for acting, it can act or not act, and do this or that. Others deny that any such indifference is included in freedom or has anything to do with it.

source_text: XXIV. Nam qui volunt libertatem non esse sine aliqua agentis liberi indifferentia, per indifferentiam non intelligunt eum statum in quo agens non inclinat in unam partem magis quam in aliam, sed stat in ancipiti aequali momento huc illuc impellendum quod contrasentientes maxime aversantur. Nec enim ullus est eorum qui tuentur istam indifferentiam, qui non censeat illam in eo quoque reperiri, qui firmo certoque judicio hoc & non aliud sibi agendum esse constituit: & cujus quoque voluntas, habitibus alte radicatis, & quos aegerrime excutere potest, in hanc, aut illam partem vehementissime fertur. Adeoque nomine indifferentiae, in hoc negotio, non aliud designant, quam potentiam veram & intrinsecam non tantum agendi, sed & ab actione cessandi, non tantum hoc agendi, sed & diversum, vel oppositum ejus. Quae potentia non solum in eo reperitur qui dubius & anceps est an agat, vel non agat, sed in eo etiam qui nullo modo haesitat & dubitat de eo quod sibi agendum sive non agendum est, quique proposito fixo, & immoto ad sic & non aliter agendum sese determinat.
english: Those who hold that freedom never exists without some indifference in the free agent do not mean by indifference a state in which the agent leans no more one way than the other and hangs in the balance, equally ready to be pushed either way. That is the very thing their opponents most object to.

None of the defenders of this indifference fails to hold that it is present even in someone who has decided, with firm and sure judgment, that he must do this and nothing else, and whose will is carried with great force in one direction by deep-rooted habits he could shake off only with the utmost difficulty.

In this matter, then, by indifference they mean simply a real, intrinsic power not only to act but also to stop acting, not only to do this but also to do something else or its opposite. That power is found not only in someone who is unsure and torn over whether to act, but also in someone who has no hesitation or doubt about what he should or should not do, and who sets himself, with a fixed and steady purpose, to act in this way and no other.

source_text: XXV. Ac praeterea quum dicunt agens liberum, positis omnibus ad agendum praerequisitis, posse agere vel non agere, hoc, aut illud agere, mens eorum non est quod positis omnibus quae ad aliquem actum voluntatis praerequiruntur, inter quae locum habet gratiae divinae motio, & practicae mentis judicium, possit actio voluntatis non sequi, & sic carentia actionis ejus jungi cum omnibus illis per quae voluntas ad agendum movetur atque disponitur. Fatentur enim impossibile esse ut Deus hominem quempiam gratia sua efficaci ad aliquem actum pietatis moveat, & tamen actus ille ab eo non eliciatur: aut ut aliquis, omnibus expensis, judicet hic & nunc istud sibi agendum & appetendum esse, & tamen idem istud non agat & appetat; Verum id solum sibi volunt illum qui, qua jam dictum est ratione, ad agendum movetur, licet infallibiliter & certo acturus sit, & contingere non possit ut non agat; illum, inquam, nihilominus veram in se retinere potentiam non agendi, & aliter agendi, quae manet non solum in eo qui proxime ad agendum paratus & dispositus est, sed in eo ipso qui jam de facto agit; quoniam etsi cum actu aliquo stare non possit ejus carentia, aut actus contrarius, optime tamen cum eo componi potest potentia ad actum illum contrarium, ut jam pluries inculcatum fuit.
english: Further, when they say that a free agent, given everything required beforehand for acting, can act or not act, and do this or that, they do not mean that the will's act can fail to follow once everything required for some act of will is in place, including the motion of God's grace and the practical judgment of the mind, so that the absence of the act could coexist with everything that moves and disposes the will to act.

They admit it is impossible for God to move someone by his effective grace to an act of godliness and for that act not to be produced, or for someone, having weighed everything, to judge that he must do and seek something here and now and then not do and seek it.

All they mean is this. The man who is moved to act in the way described will act infallibly and surely, and it cannot happen that he does not act; yet he still keeps in himself a real power not to act and to act otherwise. That power remains not only in someone fully prepared and ready to act but in someone actually acting. For although an act cannot coexist with its own absence or with a contrary act, the power to the contrary act can perfectly well coexist with it, as has been stressed many times already.

source_text: XXVI. Qui vero contra pugnant ad libertatem arbitrii non requiri aliquam agentis indifferentiam, indifferentiae nomine significare videntur voluntatis ἰσοῤῥοπίαν, quum in hanc partem non magis quam in aliam propendet, & huc non magis quam illuc flexilis est, qua in re nullus eorum qui in Scholis Christianis Theologi nomen ferunt, libertatem unquam constituit.
english: Those who argue the other way, that freedom of choice does not require any indifference in the agent, seem to mean by indifference the will's equal balance (ἰσοῤῥοπία), when it leans no more to one side than to the other and can be swayed no more this way than that.
Yet no one who bears the name of theologian in the Christian Schools has ever made freedom consist in that.

source_text: XXVII. Et similiter quum dicunt falsum esse quod agens liberum, positis omnibus quae sunt ad agendum requisita, possit agere, & non agere, hoc & illud agere, sententia eorum non est, per ea quae ad agendum praeparant & impellunt, ab agente libero tolli facultatem aliter agendi, aut actionem suspendendi: quandoquidem agnoscunt facultatem illam per actum ipsum non tolli; nedum per ea quae ad agendum impellunt. Nec enim negant eum qui per Dei gratiam egentis miseretur, in se semper habere potestatem non miserendi, & qui mundi hujus voluptates contemnit, retinere facultatem illas quaerendi atque amplectendi, quae per divinam gratiam ab eo non aufertur. Adeoque non aliud intendunt quam hoc, positis omnibus quae requiruntur ad agendum, contingere non posse ut agens liberum non agat: licet alioqui maneat in eo facultas qua posset non agere, aut aliter agere. Exempli gratia, fieri non posse quin positis omnibus quae ex parte Dei necessaria sunt ad fidem & conversionem hominis producendam, homo convertatur & credat; quanquam semper, & etiam quum credit & convertitur, in eo maneat facultas, qua non credere & non converti posset.
english: In the same way, when they say it is false that a free agent, given everything required for acting, can act and not act, and do this and that, they do not mean that whatever prepares and drives him to act takes away his ability to act otherwise or to hold the act back. They acknowledge that the act itself does not remove that ability, much less the things that drive him to it.

They do not deny that someone who by God's grace shows mercy to the needy always keeps in himself the power not to show it, or that someone who scorns this world's pleasures keeps the ability to pursue and embrace them; God's grace does not take that ability from him.

Their only point is that once everything required for acting is in place, a free agent cannot fail to act, even though he otherwise keeps an ability by which he could refrain or act differently. For instance, once everything needed on God's side to produce a man's faith and conversion is in place, the man cannot fail to be converted and believe, though always, even while he believes and is converted, he keeps an ability by which he could fail to believe and be converted.

source_text: XXVIII. Unde patet hos Theologos, quum negant libertatem consistere in quadam agentis indifferentia, duo tantum ob oculos habere, quorum unum est libertatem non consistere in ejus qui liber dicitur ancipiti statu, in quo non magis inclinat & propendet ad agendum, quam ad non agendum: alterum, posita gratiae & providentiae divinae motione & efficacia, & etiam proprii judicii dictamine, contingere non posse ut agens liberum non agat id ad quod, tum efficaci illa motione Dei, tum judicio proprio, impellitur; quod utrumque ultro fatentur illi ex Reformatis qui docent arbitrii libertate includi quandam ad agendum indifferentiam. Et Rursus ex dictis non minus evidens est Doctores illos qui tuentur istam indifferentiam hoc solum in animo habere quod divina motio, & practicae mentis judicium sic hominem ad agendum movent, ut ex una parte quidem certo & infallibiliter agat, ex altera tamen non tollatur ab eo facultas non agendi, aut aliter agendi. Non secus ac quum homo reipsa agit, eadem facultas non tollitur ab eo per actum ipsum ad quem motus & impulsus est.
english: This makes it plain that when these theologians deny that freedom consists in some indifference of the agent, they have only two things in view. First, freedom does not consist in a wavering state in which the person called free leans no more toward acting than toward not acting. Second, once God's grace and providence are at work with their motion and efficacy, and the agent's own judgment has given its dictate, the free agent cannot fail to do what God's effective motion and his own judgment drive him to. Both points are readily admitted by those Reformed who teach that freedom of choice includes a certain indifference toward acting.

What has been said shows just as clearly that the teachers who defend that indifference have only this in mind: God's motion and the mind's practical judgment move a man to act in such a way that, on the one hand, he acts surely and infallibly and, on the other, he is not deprived of the ability not to act or to act otherwise. In the same way, when a man actually acts, the act he has been moved and driven to does not take that ability from him.

source_text: XXIX. Ex omnibus autem hisce manifestum est Reformatorum hac in parte doctrinam recte expositam atque intellectam, & ex mente eorum a quibus proponitur, reipsa non differre a sententia eorum qui in Schola Romana receptiores Thomistae appellantur. Quamvis enim contendant libertatem opponi non coactioni solum, sed necessitati quoque naturali & proprie dictae, nihilominus agnoscunt positis omnibus quae sunt ad agendum praerequisita, necessario sequi actum creaturae liberae necessitate quadam infallibilitatis. Quia licet agens liberum semper in se retineat potestatem non agendi, etiam quum reipsa agit, & a fortiori quum est in proximo ad agendum; positis tamen omnibus quae, tum ex parte Dei, tum ex parte intellectus praerequiruntur ut voluntas agat, agit illa certo & infallibiliter, & impossibile est actionem ejus non sequi. Nempe ex eorum doctrina, cum omnibus illis quae sunt ad agendum praerequisita optime conjungi & consistere potest potentia non agendi, aut aliter agendi, non tamen carentia actus, & multo minus actus contrarius.
english: From all this it is clear that the Reformed teaching on this point, correctly stated and understood as its own exponents intend it, does not in fact differ from the view of those in the Roman School called the more widely received Thomists.

These Thomists maintain that freedom is opposed not only to compulsion but also to natural necessity, necessity in the proper sense. Even so, they recognize that once everything required for acting is in place, the free creature's act follows necessarily, with a necessity of infallibility.

A free agent always keeps in itself the power not to act, even while it is actually acting, and all the more when it is on the point of acting. But once everything required on God's side and on the intellect's side for the will to act is in place, the will acts surely and infallibly, and its action cannot fail to follow. On their teaching, then, the power not to act or to act otherwise can perfectly well coexist with everything required for acting, but the absence of the act cannot, and still less a contrary act.

source_text: XXX. Adeoque per indifferentiam ad agendum, vel non agendum, in qua ex eorum mente libertas constituenda est, aut quae saltem libertati est necessario juncta, non aliam intelligunt, quam quae supra jam descripta fuit. Nimirum neque talem per quam causa libera concipiatur dubia & anceps an agat, vel non agat; neque etiam per quam positis omnibus quae sunt ad agendum requisita, contingere possit ut agens liberum tam non agat, quam agat; sed quae non aliud sit quam vera non agendi, & aliter agendi potestas, quae manet in causa libera quum positis omnibus quae ad agendum requiruntur, non solum est in proximo ut agat, sed etiam infallibiliter & certo actura est, prout Alvarez suam hac de re sententiam clare admodum & diserte exponit in summa operis de auxiliis divinae gratiae lib. 4. cap. 14. unde desumpta sunt verba quae ex eodem Alvarez superiori disputatione a nobis relata sunt.
english: By the indifference to acting or not acting in which, on their view, freedom must be placed, or which at least necessarily goes with freedom, they mean nothing other than what was described above.

It is not an indifference that would picture a free cause as unsure and torn over whether to act, nor one by which, given everything required for acting, the free agent might just as well not act as act. It is simply a real power not to act and to act otherwise. That power remains in a free cause when, with everything required for acting in place, it is not only on the point of acting but will act infallibly and surely.

Alvarez sets out his view on this very clearly and explicitly in the summary of his work on the helps of divine grace, book 4, chapter 14, the source of the words of his that we quoted in the preceding disputation.

source_text: XXXI. Ac profecto eandem plane hic esse sententiam Didaci istius Alvares, & aliorum qui cum eo recentiores Thomistae nuncupantur, cum sententia Doctorum Ecclesiae Reformatae, testis idoneus est Vir Doctissimus Andreas Rivetus ante annos aliquot in Academia Leydensi Professor, dum non aliis verbis quam quae sunt ex ipso Alvarez desumpta, mentem suam de arbitrii humani libertate exprimere voluit. In summa controversiarum tract. 4. quaest. 3. Fatetur enim tolerari posse definitionem liberi arbitrii per quam dicitur facultas voluntatis qua, positis omnibus ad agendum praerequisitis, possit agere, aut non agere, dummodo id intelligatur non in sensu composito, sed in sensu diviso, Nempe, inquit, si quis dicat positis omnibus antecedenter requisitis, secundum ordinem rationis, vel temporis ad actum, liberum arbitrium posse operari, vel non operari, ita videlicet, ut cum eisdem praerequisitis stet simul in libero arbitrio facultas & potentia, qua possit operari, vel non operari si vellet, ut distinguit Didacus Alvares, quia etiam motio Dei efficax qua ad talem actum voluntas determinatur, non tollit a libero arbitrio facultatem operandi illum actum vel operandi actum contrarium, sed solum efficit, quod cum liberum arbitrium possit operari vel non operari talem actum infallibiliter, libere tamen operetur illum. Quod cum facit, manet potentia ad alium, quia ad tales actus non est naturaliter determinata. Nam ut ait idem, in causa contingenti & libera, simul est potentia ad utrumque oppositum, non tamen est potentia ad opposita simul habenda, quia potentia ad actum unum, non repugnat potentiae ad actum contrarium, nec etiam repugnat actui contrario, actus autem contrarii repugnant inter se in eodem subjecto; unde liberum arbitrium creatum non solum antequam determinetur ad unum actum, sed etiam in ipso instanti, in quo determinatur a Deo, & seipsum determinat ad eundem actum, simul habet potentiam qua potest actum contrarium producere si velit, non tamen ad actum contrarium simul habendum, quia duo actus contrarii simul in eadem potentia esse non possunt, sed successive. Quae omnia verba ex Didaco Alvarez vel expresse citata, vel saltem mutuata sunt, ut & illud quod subjungit tanquam ejusdem doctoris conclusionem quae ipsi probatur, nempe, non esse de ratione liberi arbitrii aut definitione ejus, quod positis omnibus secundum ordinem causalitatis antecedenter praerequisitis ad operandum talem actum, possit eundem actum non operari in sensu composito, si compositio fiat inter hujusmodi praerequisita, & carentiam talis actus, seu actum contrarium, id est, cum auxilio Dei efficaci, non simul stare quod liberum arbitrium non producat actum dilectionis, aut eliciat actum dilectioni Dei contrarium.
english: That the view of this Diego Alvarez, and of the others called with him the more recent Thomists, is here exactly the same as that of the teachers of the Reformed Church is well attested by the very learned Andrew Rivet, some years ago professor at the University of Leiden. When he set out his own mind on the freedom of human choice, he used no words but those taken from Alvarez himself, in his Summa of controversies, treatise 4, question 3.

He grants that one may accept the definition of free choice as 'a faculty of the will by which, given everything required beforehand for acting, it can act or not act', provided this is taken in the divided sense, not the composite. 'That is,' he says, 'if someone says that, given everything required beforehand for the act in the order of reason or of time, free choice can act or not act, meaning that together with those same prerequisites there is in free choice the ability and power by which it could act or not act if it wished, as Diego Alvarez distinguishes. For even God's effective motion, by which the will is determined to such an act, does not take from free choice the ability to perform that act or the contrary one; it only brings it about that, while free choice is able to perform such an act or not, it performs it infallibly and yet freely. When it does so, the power to another act remains, because it is not determined by nature to such acts.

For, as the same author says, in a contingent and free cause there is at once a power to either of two opposites, but not a power to have the opposites at once. A power to one act does not conflict with a power to the contrary act, nor even with the contrary act itself, though contrary acts do conflict with each other in the same subject. Hence created free choice, not only before it is determined to one act but in the very instant in which God determines it and it determines itself to that act, has at the same moment a power by which it can produce the contrary act if it wishes. It has no power to have the contrary act at the same moment, because two contrary acts cannot be in the same power at once, only one after the other.'

All these words are either quoted outright or at least borrowed from Diego Alvarez. So is what Rivet adds as that teacher's conclusion, which he endorses: that it does not belong to the nature or definition of free choice that, given everything required beforehand in the order of causality for performing such an act, it can leave that same act undone in the composite sense, if the composition is made between those prerequisites and the absence of the act or a contrary act. In other words, with God's effective help it cannot at the same time be true that free choice does not produce the act of love, or that it produces an act contrary to the love of God.

source_text: XXXII. Nulla ergo Reformatis controversia superest, quae realis sit & alicujus momenti, nisi cum iis qui in Schola Romana Molinistae dicuntur, denominatione sumpta a Ludovico Molina Jesuita celeberrimo, qui ante annos centum circiter scripsit & docuit. Quippe indifferentiam ad agendum & non agendum, in qua libertas arbitrii consistit, & vulgatam definitionem per quam dicitur esse id quo, positis omnibus ad agendum praerequisitis, potest voluntas agere & non agere, hoc aut illud agere, longe aliter intelligunt quam Thomistae recentiores, ut praecedenti disputatione manifestum fecimus.
english: So no dispute of substance or of any weight is left for the Reformed except with those in the Roman School called Molinists, after the famous Jesuit Luis de Molina, who wrote and taught about a century ago.

They understand the indifference to acting and not acting in which freedom of choice consists, and the familiar definition that calls it 'that by which, given everything required beforehand for acting, the will can act and not act, do this or that', very differently from the more recent Thomists, as we showed in the preceding disputation.

source_text: XXXIII. Fatentur quidem cum aliis per indifferentiam de qua hic quaestio est, non significari eam voluntatis constitutionem per quam non magis huc propendeat quam illuc, sed inter duo opposita haereat, quasi suspensa in aequilibrio: cum agnoscant libertati nihil praejudicari per habitus quibus voluntas ad hoc potius quam illud agendum fortiter inclinatur, & difficulter alio ferri potest. Et praeterea non negant in sensu quodam composito falsum esse quod voluntas possit agere & non agere, hoc & illud agere; nempe, si quis per hoc significari putet actum & ejus carentiam, aut duos actus contrarios in voluntate simul stare & componi posse. Admittunt quoque per indifferentiam in qua libertatis essentia consistit, non intelligi potestatem bene vel male agendi. Agnoscunt enim libertatem arbitrii manere etiam in eo qui non potest bene agere, ut in spiritibus damnatis: & multo magis adhuc illam in eo reperiri qui male agere non potest, ut in sanctis qui faciem Dei vident, & cum eo in coelo regnant.
english: They do agree with the others that the indifference in question here does not mean a condition of the will in which it leans no more one way than the other and hangs between two opposites as if balanced on scales. They grant that freedom suffers nothing from habits that strongly incline the will to do this rather than that and make it hard for it to go another way.

Nor do they deny that, in a certain composite sense, it is false that the will can act and not act, or do this and that, namely if someone takes this to mean that an act and its absence, or two contrary acts, can be present and combined in the will at once.

They also accept that the indifference in which the essence of freedom consists is not the power to act well or badly. They acknowledge that freedom of choice remains even in one who cannot act well, as in the damned spirits, and is present still more in one who cannot act badly, as in the saints who see God's face and reign with him in heaven.

source_text: XXXIV. Sed acriter defendunt voluntatem in se sic indeterminatam & indifferentem esse, ut positis omnibus ad agendum praerequisitis, sive ex parte Dei, sive ex parte objecti, sive ex parte intellectus, fieri possit & saepe etiam eveniat, ut voluntas non agat: adeoque nihil esse eorum quae voluntatem antecedenter ad agendum movent atque incitant, quo posito non possit voluntatis actio non sequi, & saepius etiam reapse non sequatur: & sic cum omnibus illis quae actionem voluntatis praecedunt, & ad eam praerequiruntur, revera conjungi & componi posse, non solum potestatem ad non agendum aut aliud agendum, sed ipsam actus carentiam, & actum quoque contrarium. Quod negant, ut satis liquet ex antedictis, non solum Reformati, verum etiam Thomistae illi recentiores. Quippe sentiunt cum iis quae vel ex parte Dei, vel ex parte intellectus ad agendum necessaria sunt, posse quidem in voluntate consistere potestatem non agendi, vel agendi oppositum; sed tamen iis positis voluntatem semper agere, nec fieri posse ut aliter eveniat: quoniam ex hac hypothesi voluntas agit certo & infallibiliter, licet in se retineat non agendi potentiam.
english: What they do defend, and strongly, is that the will is in itself so undetermined and indifferent that, given everything required beforehand for acting, whether on God's side, the object's, or the intellect's, the will can fail to act, and often actually does. Nothing, then, that moves and stirs the will to act beforehand is such that, once it is in place, the will's act cannot fail to follow; quite often it really does not follow.

So everything that precedes the will's act and is required for it can really be combined not only with a power not to act or to do something else but with the very absence of the act, and even with the contrary act.

As the foregoing shows clearly enough, both the Reformed and those more recent Thomists deny this. They hold that a power not to act, or to do the opposite, can indeed coexist in the will with what God's side or the intellect's side requires for acting, but that once those are in place the will always acts and nothing else can happen. On that supposition the will acts surely and infallibly, though it keeps in itself the power not to act.

source_text: XXXV. Porro cum lis ista apud Romanos Pontifices, & coetum Cardinalium ad hoc deputatorum saepe fuerit mota & agitata, hactenus tamen illam nondum definierunt, & licitum suis esse voluerunt hanc aut illam sententiam pro arbitrio tenere & tueri. Quanquam sicut sub hujus saeculi initium & praecedentis finem Thomistarum sententiae favere visi sunt Romani Pontifices Paulus V. & Clemens VIII. Sic postremis hisce annis oppositae doctrinae magis favisse videntur eorum successores Innocentius X. & Alexander VII. Unde factum est ut jam in Schola Romana longe communior evaserit, & a maxima parte Theologorum teneatur.
english: The dispute has often been raised and argued before the popes of Rome and before a body of cardinals appointed for the purpose, yet so far they have not settled it, and they have allowed their people to hold and defend either view as they choose.

Around the turn of this century, at the close of the last, Popes Paul V and Clement VIII seemed to favour the Thomists' view. In these last years their successors Innocent X and Alexander VII seem to have leaned rather toward the opposite teaching. As a result it has now become by far the more common view in the Roman School and is held by most of its theologians.

source_text: XXXVI. Ac praeterea sicut hac in parte communibus armis Molinistas impugnant cum Reformatis illis qui Dordracenae Synodo subscribunt, nonnulli Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, ut qui vocantur Jansenistae, & Thomistae illi quoque recentiores: sic a parte Molinistarum stant, & eorum in hac quaestione doctrinam acerrime defendunt illi ex Reformatis qui in Belgio dicuntur Remonstrantes sive Arminiani, aliique qui Dordracenam Synodum non sequuntur.
english: On this point, moreover, some teachers of the Roman Church, namely the so-called Jansenists and those more recent Thomists as well, join forces against the Molinists with the Reformed who subscribe to the Synod of Dort.

On the Molinists' side, by contrast, stand those Reformed in the Netherlands called Remonstrants or Arminians, along with others who do not follow the Synod of Dort, and they defend the Molinist teaching on this question very vigorously.

source_text: XXXVII. Eorum autem sententia hoc praecipue nomine a Scholae Reformatae Doctoribus rejicitur quod divinae gratiae efficaciam minuit, & libero arbitrio plus tribuit quam par est in salutis negotio. Etenim scriptura docente, quicquid in nobis boni est, in solidum divinae gratiae acceptum ferri debet; juxta illud Apostoli, Quid habes quod non accepisti? sed ex ista doctrina sequitur, quod homo possit credere & Deum diligere, tribuendum esse quidem gratiae auxiliis, hominem ad fidem & dilectionem moventibus & excitantibus, verum quod homo gratiae moventi consentiat & ad credendum & Deum diligendum sese determinet, sic a libertate arbitrii pendere ut gratiae divinae proprie effectus non sit, quandoquidem posita gratia consensus ille saepe non consequitur; & ita gratia divina dici potest tantum ejus conditio, vel causa sine qua non.
english: The Reformed teachers reject their view mainly because it lessens the efficacy of God's grace and gives free choice more than its due in the matter of salvation.

Scripture teaches that every good thing in us must be credited entirely to God's grace, as the Apostle says: 'What do you have that you did not receive?' On this teaching, however, the fact that a man is able to believe and love God is indeed owed to the helps of grace, which move and stir him to faith and love. But the fact that he consents to the grace that moves him and settles himself to believe and love God depends so much on his freedom of choice that it is not, properly, an effect of God's grace, since the consent often fails to follow when grace is given. God's grace could then be called only a condition of it, a cause without which it would not happen.

source_text: XXXVIII. Praeterea scriptura docet gratiam divinam esse quae discrimen inter homines ponit, inter eos scilicet qui convertuntur & qui non convertuntur, inter credentes atque incredulos inter eos qui Deo vocanti parent & eos qui illi resistunt: secundum illud Pauli, Quis te discernit? sed ex doctrina eorum de quibus jam agimus, sequitur non gratiam divinam; sed simpliciter voluntatem humanam hoc discrimen inter homines constituere. Supponit enim aequali gratia pluribus oblata, hunc credere; illum non credere; hunc converti, illum non converti: Et consequenter quod hic potius quam ille credit & convertitur, ad aliquam gratiae efficaciam referri non debere, sed solum ad liberam voluntatis humanae determinationem; quia nimirum hic gratiae moventi & praevenienti consentire voluit, ille vero noluit.
english: Scripture also teaches that it is God's grace that sets people apart from one another: those who are converted from those who are not, believers from unbelievers, those who obey God's call from those who resist it. As Paul says, 'Who makes you different?'

The doctrine we are now examining, however, implies that the difference between people is made not by God's grace but simply by the human will. It assumes that when equal grace is offered to several people, one believes and another does not, one is converted and another is not.

It follows that one person's believing and being converted rather than another's must be traced not to any efficacy of grace but only to the free self-determination of the human will, because this one chose to consent to the grace that moved him and came first to him, while that one refused.

source_text: XXXIX. Adde quod si gratia divina sic tantum homines movet, praeparat & incitat ad volendum & perficiendum ea quae Deus jubet, ut tamen ipsum velle & perficere, ea posita, possit in homine non sequi, & de facto saepe non sequatur, operatur illa quidem in homine vires seu dispositiones necessarias ad bonum volendum & perficiendum, non autem ipsum velle & perficere. Sed Apostolus contra testatur, Deum esse qui operatur in nobis & velle & perficere pro bona voluntate. Phil. 2. 13.
english: Moreover, if God's grace merely moves, prepares and stirs people to will and to carry out what he commands, in such a way that the willing and doing themselves can fail to follow in a person once grace is given, and in fact often do fail, then grace produces in a person the strength or the dispositions needed for willing and doing good, but not the willing and doing themselves.
The Apostle testifies the opposite: it is God who works in us both to will and to do for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:13).

source_text: XL. Denique si positis omnibus ad agendum praerequisitis, etiam ex parte Dei, non exclusa qualibet gratiae efficacia, semper contingere potest ut voluntas non agat, nulla datur Dei gratia, saltem ordinaria, quam infallibiliter & certo sequatur hominis conversio, & qua qui donantur omnes, nullo excepto, ad Christum veniant. Sed contra Christus ipse docet esse quandam Dei gratiam, quam nemo accipit qui non veniat ad ipsum. Nam quicunque, inquit, audivit & didicit a Patre venit ad me. Joannis capite sexto.
english: Finally, if the will can always fail to act even when everything required for acting is in place, on God's side too and with no efficacy of grace whatever left out, then there is no grace of God, at least no ordinary grace, that a person's conversion follows infallibly and surely, and that brings everyone who receives it, without exception, to Christ.
Christ himself teaches the opposite: there is a grace of God that no one receives without coming to him. 'Everyone,' he says, 'who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me' (John 6).

source_text: XLI. Et certe si multi eorum qui per Patris gratiam trahuntur & intus a Deo docentur, in Christum tamen non credunt, nec ad eum veniunt, quomodo Christus ibidem hanc rationem afferret cur non omnes qui audiunt Evangelium ad ipsum veniant; quod, scilicet, necesse sit illos qui ad ipsum veniunt a Patre trahi & doceri? Nolite, inquit, murmurare inter vos. Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi Pater qui misit me traxerit eum. Est scriptum in Prophetis, Et erunt omnes docti a Deo. Omnis ergo qui audivit a Patre & didicit venit ad me. Profecto si illi ipsi qui non credunt Evangelio per Patris gratiam trahuntur, absurdum esset dicere, Ne miremini quod isti & illi quibus praedicatum fuit Evangelium in Evangelium tamen non crediderunt; quoniam necesse est eos qui credunt in Evangelium per gratiam divinam trahi.
english: Surely, if many of those whom the Father's grace draws and God teaches inwardly still do not believe in Christ or come to him, how could Christ give, in that same passage, this as the reason why not everyone who hears the gospel comes to him, namely that those who come to him must be drawn and taught by the Father?

'Do not grumble among yourselves,' he says. 'No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. It is written in the Prophets: And they will all be taught by God. Everyone, then, who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me.'

If the very people who do not believe the gospel are drawn by the Father's grace, it would make no sense to say: 'Do not be surprised that this person and that, to whom the gospel was preached, have still not believed it, since those who believe the gospel must be drawn by God's grace.'

source_text: XLII. Cum ergo sit quaedam divina gratia, & quidem electis omnibus communis, ad cujus motionem atque impulsionem hominis conversio infallibiliter & certo consequitur; & tamen omnium consensu conversio hominis ad Deum sit liber voluntatis actus: planum est libertatem in eo male constitui, quod positis omnibus ad agendum praerequisitis ipsaque ordinaria gratiae motione, voluntas semper possit tam non agere quam agere, non tantum in sensu diviso sed in sensu quoque composito, ita ut cum illa gratiae motione conjungi possit carentia actus ad quem hominem movet.
english: There is, then, a divine grace, shared indeed by all the elect, whose motion and impulse a person's conversion follows infallibly and surely; and yet everyone agrees that a person's conversion to God is a free act of the will.

It is clear, therefore, that freedom is wrongly located in the will's always being able, with everything required for acting in place, including grace's ordinary motion, as much not to act as to act, and that not only in the divided sense but also in the composite sense, so that grace's motion could coexist with the absence of the act toward which it moves a person.

source_text: XLIII. Itaque vulgata illa descriptione Liberi Arbitrii per quam definitur facultas qua positis omnibus ad agendum praerequisitis, potest aliquis agere & non agere, hoc aut illud agere, tutior est ea quam substituit Alvarez, Liberum arbitrium est facultas voluntatis & rationis ad utrum libet agendum vel non agendum & agendum unum vel alterum. Aut etiam illa Bellarmini, Liberum arbitrium est libera potestas ex his quae ad finem aliquem conducunt unum prae alio eligendi, aut unum & idem respuendi vel acceptandi pro arbitrio nostro, ad magnam Dei gloriam attributa vel concessa.
english: So, rather than the familiar description of free choice as 'a faculty by which, given everything required beforehand for acting, a person can act and not act, do this or that', it is safer to use the one Alvarez put in its place: 'Free choice is a faculty of will and reason for acting or not acting, as one pleases, and for doing one thing or the other.'

Or else Bellarmine's: 'Free choice is a free power, given or granted for the great glory of God, to choose one thing over another among the things that lead to some end, or to reject or accept one and the same thing as we decide.'
